questions.question_text: Pica

options.text: is usually diagnosed most easily when the child is younger than 2 years of age
decreases in prevalence with increasing severity of mental retardation
is not diagnosed if symptoms occur in the context of another disorder, including schizophrenia and autistic disorder
is diagnosed even if symptoms are culturally accepted
none of the above

questions.explanation:
The DSM-IV-TR describes pica as the persistent eating of nonnutritive substances for at least 1 month[cite: 4]. The behavior must be developmentally inappropriate, not culturally sanctioned, and sufficiently severe to merit clinical attention[cite: 4]. Under these circumstances, pica is diagnosed even when symptoms occur in the context of another mental disorder, such as schizophrenia, autistic disorder, or Kleine-Levin syndrome[cite: 4].
Pica occurs more frequently in young children than in adults and is more common in individuals with mental retardation[cite: 4]. Forms of pica, including geophagia (clay eating) and amylophagia (starch eating), do occur among adults, particularly pregnant women[cite: 4]. According to DSM-IV-TR criteria, if such practices are culturally sanctioned, diagnostic criteria for pica are not met[cite: 4].
Because infants commonly mouth objects as part of their exploration of their environment, it is difficult to diagnose pica in children younger than age 2 years[cite: 4]. Among individuals with mental retardation, the prevalence of pica appears to increase with the severity of the retardation[cite: 4].

questions.question_text: A diagnosis of rumination disorder

options.text: is commonly made in older children and adolescents
cannot be made in individuals with mental retardation or a pervasive developmental disorder
cannot be attributable to an associated gastrointestinal condition
is not made in children with a prior period of normal functioning
occurs more often in females than in males

correct_answer.text: cannot be attributable to an associated gastrointestinal condition

correct_answers.text: cannot be attributable to an associated gastrointestinal condition

questions.explanation: The DSM-IV-TR describes rumination disorder as behavior by an infant or child in which food is repeatedly regurgitated or rechewed[cite: 4]. The behavior must occur after a period of normal functioning, take place for at least 1 month, and not be attributable to a gastrointestinal or other medical condition[cite: 4]. The onset of the disorder typically occurs after 3 months of age[cite: 4]. Infants who ruminate are observed to strain to bring food back into their mouths and appear to derive pleasure from the behavior[cite: 4]. After regurgitation, the food is swallowed, chewed, or spit out[cite: 4]. The infants often come to clinical attention because of failure to thrive[cite: 4]. Even in the context of other mental disorders, such as mental retardation or pervasive developmental disorders, the diagnosis of rumination disorder may be made if the symptoms are sufficiently severe to warrant clinical attention[cite: 4]. The disorder is rare in older children and adolescents and occurs more often in males than in females and individuals with mental retardation[cite: 4].

questions.question_text: Behaviors which may be related to pica include

options.text: nail biting
thumb sucking
delays in speech and psychosocial development
bulimia nervosa
all of the above

questions.explanation: Many children with pica engage in other oral activities that likely have self-soothing effects, including thumb sucking and nail biting[cite: 4]. Typically, pica occurs for several months and then remits[cite: 4]. However, a minority of cases continues through childhood and adolescence and even into adulthood[cite: 4]. Several authors have highlighted significant impact associated with long-standing pica, including delays in speech and psychosocial development, depression, ongoing disturbed oral activities (thumb sucking, nail biting), and tobacco and other substance abuse[cite: 4]. Additionally, some authors have identified a relationship between pica during early childhood and bulimia nervosa during adolescence[cite: 4].

questions.question_text: Feeding disorder of infancy or early childhood

options.text: has narrow DSM-IV-TR diagnostic criteria that address the specificity of various feeding disorders
has been reported in 1 to 2 percent of infants and toddlers
may have an age of onset after 6 years
does not necessarily result in significant failure to gain weight
none of the above

correct_answer.text: has been reported in 1 to 2 percent of infants and toddlers

correct_answers.text: has been reported in 1 to 2 percent of infants and toddlers

questions.explanation:
According to DSM-IV-TR criteria, feeding disorder of infancy or early childhood is a persistent failure to eat adequately, resulting in significant failure to gain weight or in significant weight loss over at least 1 month[cite: 4]. The symptoms are not better accounted for by a medical condition, another mental disorder, or lack of food, and the disorder’s onset must occur before (not after) age 6 years[cite: 4]. The DSM-IV-TR criteria are broad (not narrow) and do not address the specificity of feeding disorders that are not separately included in the DSM-IV or ICD-10[cite: 4].
An estimated 15 to 35 percent of infants and young children have feeding difficulties; common problems include eating too little, refusing certain foods, objectionable mealtime behaviors, and bizarre food habits[cite: 4]. However, these problems tend to be mild and do not significantly impact the child’s growth[cite: 4]. Severe feeding problems associated with poor weight gain are reported in 1 to 2 percent of infants and toddlers[cite: 4].

questions.question_text: Susan was admitted to the hospital at age 6 months for evaluation of failure to gain weight. She had been born into an impoverished family after an unplanned, uncomplicated pregnancy. During her first 4 months of life, she gained weight steadily. Beginning in her fifth month, she was noted to regurgitate milk after feedings. She would then vigorously suck her thumb and other fingers, and milk would continue to be regurgitated into her mouth. Her weight leveled off and then began to decrease during this time. In the 2 months before the onset of this behavior, Susan had multiple caregivers and received little attention from her parents. Nevertheless, she smiled often and was responsive to all of her caregivers. The most likely diagnosis is

options.text: rumination disorder
reactive attachment disorder
pica
failure to thrive
none of the above

questions.explanation: Failure to gain weight or weight loss in an infant, after general medical conditions have been ruled out, suggests rumination disorder of infancy, feeding disorder of infancy or early childhood, or reactive attachment disorder of infancy or early childhood[cite: 4]. The child in this case is not gaining weight because of the regurgitation of food after each feeding, indicating a diagnosis of rumination disorder of infancy[cite: 4]. Typically, the child strains and makes sucking noises with the tongue to regurgitate food and then rechews or reswallows the food[cite: 4]. Often, the child gives the impression of deriving considerable satisfaction from the behavior[cite: 4]. The disorder usually occurs between 3 and 12 months of age[cite: 4]. There is a suggestion in this case that parental care may be inadequate, but the absence of evidence of inappropriate social relatedness rules out the diagnosis of reactive attachment disorder of early childhood[cite: 4]. Because the cause of the weight loss is the regurgitation, the general diagnosis of feeding disorder of infancy or early childhood is not made[cite: 4]. Pica is the craving and eating of nonfood substances, such as paint, clay, or dirt[cite: 4]. In failure to thrive, an infant shows physical signs of malnourishment and does not exhibit the expected developmental motor and verbal milestones[cite: 4].

questions.question_text: Thomas was 3 months old when he was referred for a psychiatric evaluation because of his feeding difficulties and poor weight gain since birth. His parents were college educated, and both had pursued their professional careers until Thomas was born. Although Thomas was full term and weighed 7 pounds at birth, he had difficulty drinking from the breast. When he was 4 weeks old, his mother had reluctantly switched him to bottle feedings because he was losing weight. Although his intake improved somewhat on bottle feedings, he gained weight very slowly and was still less than 8 pounds at 3 months of age. His mother appeared tired and described how Thomas would drink only 1, 2, or 3 oz at a time, wiggle and cry, and refuse to continue with the feeding. The observation of mother–infant interactions during feeding and play revealed that Thomas was a very alert and wiggly baby who had difficulty settling in his mother’s arms. Thomas would most likely be characterized with

options.text: pica
rumination disorder
feeding disorder of state regulation
feeding disorder of caregiver–infant reciprocity
infantile anorexia

questions.explanation:
Judging by his inability to relax and stay still long enough to feed and the irregularity of his feedings, Thomas can be diagnosed with feeding disorder of state regulation[cite: 4]. Feeding disorder of state regulation begins in the postnatal period and is characterized by irregular, poor feeding and inadequate food intake by the infant[cite: 4]. Infants with this disorder have difficulty reaching and maintaining a state of calm alertness necessary for feeding[cite: 4]. Some infants are too irritable and cry excessively and cannot calm themselves for feeding, and others are too sleepy and cannot wake up or stay awake long enough to feed adequately[cite: 4]. The parent may be anxious or depressed or may present with more severe psychopathology[cite: 4]. Mother–infant interactions during feeding are characterized by irritability or sleepiness of the infant, maternal tension, and poor engagement between the mother and infant[cite: 4].
Young children with pica typically eat plaster, paper, paint, cloth, hair, insects, animal droppings, sand, pebbles, or dirt[cite: 4]. Rumination disorder is defined as repetitive regurgitation of gastric contents that are subsequently rechewed and then swallowed or ejected by the mouth[cite: 4]. Feeding disorder of caregiver–infant reciprocity is characterized by a lack of engagement between the mother and infant, leading to inadequate food intake and growth failure of the infant[cite: 4]. The onset of the growth failure is usually between 2 and 8 months of age[cite: 4]. The infant shows a lack of age-appropriate social responsivity (i.e., lack of smiling response, lack of vocal reciprocity)[cite: 4]. Infantile anorexia is characterized by a lack of appetite of the infant and inadequate food intake leading to poor weight gain and slow growth[cite: 4]. Observation of mother–infant interactions during feeding reveal that mothers and infants with this feeding disorder engage in more conflict and struggle for control during feeding and use more talk and distraction during feeding than mothers of infants without feeding problems[cite: 4].

questions.question_text: The diagnosis in the case above is frequently associated with

options.text: prematurity
gastrointestinal disease
pulmonary disease
cardiac disease
all of the above

questions.explanation: Feeding disorder of state regulation can be seen in infants without any organic problems, but it is frequently associated with prematurity or dysmaturity, and gastrointestinal, cardiac, or pulmonary disease[cite: 4].

questions.explanation:
Young children with pica typically eat plaster, paper, paint (which may cause lead poisoning), cloth, hair, animal droppings (which may cause toxoplasmosis), sand, pebbles, or dirt[cite: 4].
Rumination disorder is included under “Feeding Disorders of Infancy and Childhood” in ICD-10 but forms its own diagnostic category in DSM-IV-TR[cite: 4]. Pica is a diagnosis under both the ICD-10 and DSM-IV-TR[cite: 4].
Although rumination disorder and pica most commonly occur in infancy and early childhood, both may have their onset at any age in life, including adolescence and adulthood[cite: 4]. Rumination disorder has been reported to start later in life in adults with eating disorders[cite: 4]. In individuals with mental retardation and developmental disorders, these conditions may have onset later in life[cite: 4].
Both rumination disorder and pica have high rates of spontaneous remission[cite: 4]. Rumination disorder appears to be reinforced by pleasurable self-stimulation[cite: 4]. Frequently, vomiting secondary to acute illness or to gastroesophageal reflux precedes the onset of rumination[cite: 4]. Both pica and rumination are associated with failure to thrive; in severe cases, life-threatening malnutrition may occur with rumination[cite: 4]. Both rumination and pica are associated with adolescent- and adult-onset eating disorders[cite: 4]. Pica may occur in pregnant women and is especially prevalent during pregnancy in certain cultures[cite: 4].

questions.question_text: Toddlers with the disorder have a high level of physiological arousal.

options.text: Infantile anorexia
Sensory food aversions
Posttraumatic feeding disorder

questions.explanation:
Infantile anorexia is characterized by a lack of appetite (anorexia) of the infant and inadequate food intake leading to poor weight gain and slow growth[cite: 4]. The pattern of food refusal is usually inconsistent, depending on the mood of the child[cite: 4]. Some mothers report that even within the first 6 months of life, the infant is very responsive to environmental stimuli and stops feeding if someone enters the room, if the telephone rings, or even if the mother sneezes[cite: 4]. Toddlers with infantile anorexia have been found to have a higher level of physiological arousal and more difficulty downregulating their level of arousal[cite: 4]. This may explain why these children have so little awareness of hunger because they seem very excited by their play and are talkative and have difficulty turning away from pleasurable activities[cite: 4].
Sensory food aversions are common[cite: 4]. However, whereas some children refuse to eat only a few specific foods, others may refuse most foods and take in only a limited diet of a few foods[cite: 4]. Within this disorder, food refusal is related to the taste, texture, temperature, or smell of particular foods[cite: 4]. Children who refuse to eat vegetables and fruits usually develop vitamin deficiencies, and those who refuse to drink milk or eat meats may develop protein, zinc, or iron deficiencies[cite: 4]. In addition, children who refuse to eat foods that require more chewing (e.g., meats or hard vegetables), may present with delay in oral motor development, which may be associated with articulation difficulties[cite: 4].
The observation of infants with posttraumatic feeding disorder reveals that their food refusal seems to be caused by fear[cite: 4]. This feeding disorder may present with total food refusal, refusal to swallow solid foods, or refusal to drink from the bottle, depending on what mode of feeding the child associates with a traumatic event[cite: 4]. The onset of the food refusal is frequently rather sudden and occurs after traumatic experiences that involve the oropharynx or gastrointestinal tract (i.e., severe gagging, choking, vomiting, insertion of a feeding or endotracheal tube)[cite: 4]. Usually, food refusal is more global in posttraumatic feeding disorder than sensory food aversions, which is more selective[cite: 4]. However, sometimes children with sensory food aversions develop posttraumatic feeding disorder if they experience a strong aversive reaction or if they are force fed aversive foods that trigger gagging and vomiting[cite: 4].
